extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of evolutionary theory, social science, and philosophy of biology (readers of 19th-century evolutionary sociology)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and analysis of how single causes produce many effects in biological, psychological, and social evolution, and how uniform forces acting on heterogeneous aggregates produce segregation. Uses empirical and conceptual examples (geology, nervous system, division of labour, steam power, rivers, winnowing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of Effects as a Part-cause of Evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: “A part-cause of Evolution is the multiplication of effects; and that this increases in geometrical progression as the heterogeneity becomes greater.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument and examples show that single causes (geological mutations, famine, war, technological invention) produce many downstream changes in organisms, societies, and ideas. The book illustrates with biological divergence, breeds of domestic animals, population dispersal, and cascading social changes; emphasizes both inductive evidence and deduction from general principles (persistence of force).

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater heterogeneity increases multiplicity of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “in proportion as the area affected is complex, the number of changes multiplies” / “this multiplication increases in geometrical progression as the heterogeneity becomes greater.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a new invention (e.g., caoutchouc, electric telegraph) causes few changes in a small homogeneous tribe but multitudinous changes in an industrially heterogeneous nation; the wider and more heterogeneous the arena, the more ramified the consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensation and cognition produce multiple associated ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: “A sensation does not expend itself in arousing some single state of consciousness; but the state of consciousness aroused is made up of various represented sensations ... in proportion as the grade of intelligence is high, the number of ideas suggested is great.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the single event of spotting an unfamiliar bird, which elicits progressively more numerous and complex mental changes in (a) grazing animals, (b) a village bird-stuffer, (c) an old-school naturalist, and (d) a comparative anatomist — showing how a single stimulus branches into many intellectual consequences depending on prior development and expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional changes accumulate into structural changes
rubrics_metrics.description: “Those who recognize that the structural changes are the slowly accumulated results of the functional changes, will readily draw the corollary, that a part-cause of the evolution of the nervous system ... is this multiplication of effects.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that repeated functional/mentally-induced reactions produce gradual structural evolution (e.g., nervous-system development), so multiplication of mental/functional effects contributes causally to longer-term morphological change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labour and specialization follow from individual aptitude and exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: When some individual displays aptitude for making an article formerly produced by all, “there arises a tendency towards the differentiation of that individual into a maker of weapons,” leading to barter and further social differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chain of causal steps: individual aptitude + client demand → specialization → cessation of practice among others → increased specialization and permanence of roles → barter and wider exchanges → further development of specialities. This is used as a mechanism by which a single social cause produces many subsidiary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological innovations produce ramified social changes
rubrics_metrics.description: The locomotive engine (as proximate cause of railways) has changed country, trade, and habits of people, initiating many occupations, industries, and changes in business organization and daily life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed list of cascading effects: planning and parliamentary processes, construction trades, new classes of workers (drivers, stokers), altered commerce (wholesale/retail shifts), cheaper distribution and travel, spread of cheap literature and advertising — illustrating how one technological cause multiplies effects across society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area and scale amplify effects of causal innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: The same agent produces far fewer effects in a small homogeneous community than in a large heterogeneous one: e.g., the electric telegraph would produce scarcely any results in a small Hebridean community but multitudinous results in England.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes that the size and heterogeneity of the social/physical arena determine the breadth and complexity of downstream consequences when a new force or innovation appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of force implies dispersion and differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Our warrant is the persistence of force ... that when unlike parts of a whole react differently on a uniform incident force, the force must be differently modified ... a uniform force, falling on a uniform aggregate, must undergo dispersion; that falling on an aggregate made up of unlike parts, it must undergo dispersion from each part.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical/deductive claim: differences in reactions to uniform incident forces are attributed to differences in constituent forces (persistence of force). From this follows that uniform inputs are transformed into diverse outputs proportional to heterogeneity, thus grounding the earlier empirical claims about multiplication of effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Segregation produced by uniform forces acting on heterogeneous aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform forces acting indiscriminately on aggregates made of unlike units separate them into minor aggregates each consisting of units like to one another and unlike those of other minor aggregates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many empirical examples: wind gathering decaying leaves into eddies, winnowing chaff from wheat, river deposition sorting boulders/sand/mud, emery grading in compartments, magnetic separation of iron grains, chemical affinity separating soluble from insoluble — all illustrate the same segregative principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between mechanical motion and molecular (chemical) change determines segregation outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: If little of the incident force is absorbed in rearranging ultimate components (chemical redistribution), much must appear as motion of compound units; similar units are thus moved alike and segregate from dissimilar units moved differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanistic explanation: the partitioning of the incident (persistent) force into molecular vs. mechanical effects causes like units to experience similar motions and therefore be transferred together; conversely where chemical changes predominate, mechanical segregation is reduced. This explains when and how mixed aggregates physically separate into distinct groups.
